title: SalesSim: Benchmarking and Aligning Multimodal Language Models as Retail User Simulators

paper.title: SalesSim : Benchmarking and Aligning Multimodal Language Models as Retail User Simulators
paper.abstract:
Abstract We present SalesSim , a framework and benchmark for evaluating the ability of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to simulate realistic, persona-driven customer behavior in multi-turn, multi-modal, tool-augmented online retail conversations.
Unlike prior work that treat user simulation as surface-level dialogue generation, SalesSim models retail interaction and decision-making as a grounded, agentic process, where shoppers with diverse backgrounds, preferences, and dealbreakers interact with a sales agent, seek clarifications, and make informed purchasing decisions.
For evaluation, we design a suite of metrics centered on decision alignment, measuring the consistency between the imulator’s actions and its persona specifications, as well as conversational quality. We find several behaviorial gaps after benchmarking 6 open and closed-source state-of-the-art models. First, while models produce fluent conversations, they display significantly lower lexical diversity and overdisclosure of criterias across personas compared to human conversations. Second, models tend to be persuaded by sales agent suggestions and drift from persona specifications. Even the strongest model achieves <79% average alignment with its underlying persona specifications.
To make progress on these limitations, we propose UserGRPO , a multi-turn, multi-objective reinforcement learning recipe to optimize both conversational fluency and decision alignment under persona specifications.
Our experiments demonstrate that UserGRPO boosts decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while improving conversational quality. By introducing SalesSim , we provide a testbed for the community to investigate and improve the adherence of user simulators in goal-oriented settings.

By introducing SalesSim , we provide a testbed for the community to investigate and improve the adherence of user simulators in goal-oriented settings. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have been increasingly used as user simulators for economic simulations and evaluation and training of interactive AI systems. [ 31 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 3 , 40 , 27 , 26 , 14 , 25 , 5 ] . However, the fidelity of user simulators themselves has been relatively understudied. In this work, we study the efficacy of using Multimodal LLMs (MLLM) as customer simulators in retail interactions, inspired by economic simulations from [ 25 ] as well as product usecases such as customer simulators for sales training. Existing works assess customer simulators on surface-level qualities: [ 9 , 18 ] utilize task success rate as the main metric, which is affected by both shopper and sales agent performance. In the retail domain, Gromada et al. [12] introduces customer simulator-specific metrics that rely on rating scales and LLM-as-a-judge for persona adherence. Unlike this work, we design our evaluation methodology such that there exists a ground truth mapping between persona specifications and acceptable products in the catalog data, allowing for verifiable evaluation of decision-level persona adherence. Figure 1 : Qualitative examples of retail simulations on SalesSim . Baseline models exhibit over-leniency. They are also susceptible to tonality of the salesperson simulator, both in proceeding with unsuitable purchases or rejecting acceptable products as specified by their persona. In contrast, our UserGRPO model demonstrates more grounded reasoning based on product attributes. We introduce SalesSim , a testbed for evaluating MLLMs as persona-driven agents in multi-turn, multimodal retail interactions. SalesSim features 674 distinct shopper personas across 6 product categories of 274 rich product metadata. We evaluate model-simulated customer agents on several aspects: (1) Decision Alignment (DA) , which measures whether final actions are consistent with persona constraints; and (2) Conversational Fidelity , which measure conversational realism compared with real-world human shopper dialogues [ 16 ] . Through benchmarking state-of-the-art MLLMs, we uncover limitations of existing models to simulate realistic shoppers. While these models produce fluent outputs, they tend to be susceptible to salesperson agent suggestions. Even strong closed-source models like ChatGPT-5.4 only achieves 74.3% decision alignment rate. To address this limitation, we propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level reinforcement learning recipe that directly optimizes decision consistency under persona constraints. UserGRPO improves decision alignment of the baseline model by 13.8% while preserving linguistic quality across product domains, surpassing prompting and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines. Our contributions are three-fold: • We propose SalesSim , a grounded, multi-turn, multimodal agentic environment for benchmarking persona-driven shopper simulation. • We present empirical evidence that state-of-the-art MLLMs fail to align decisions with persona constraints despite fluent language. • We propose UserGRPO , a trajectory-level multi-turn RL recipe that improves decision alignment and corrects for unnatural information flow in retail simulations. 2 SalesSim Benchmark: Overview Figure 2 : Example of the SalesSim product and persona data. Our product data consists of rich metadata including features, prices, and multimodal information. Our persona data consists of fine-grained preferences and dealbreakers that tie closely to product choices. We propose SalesSim , an agentic simulation environment targeting retail interaction. Our framework extends from the dual-agent setup from Murakhovs’ka et al. [22] , with the ecological goal of creating realistic shopper simulators that can be used in downstream applications such as sales training, economic simulations, and evaluation and training of retail agents. 2.1 Benchmark Construction To create a diverse foundation for benchmarking model adherence to shopper behavior, we construct a benchmark of 674 consumer personas across 6 product categories, consisting of 274 information-rich product metadata describing different features (e.g. color, fabric) in high granularity. Figure 2 illustrates the personas and product specifications. 2.1.1 Product Inventory Curation To evaluate user simulation performance across diverse online retail domains, we construct our product inventory to ensure both category diversity and multimodal richness. We create a base product inventory with six product categories: Female Clothing, Male Clothing, Rings, Smart Watch, Cars, Games . We construct the base inventory by integrating real-world product data from multiple sources, such as prior recommendation and sales datasets [ 20 ] and publicly available commercial retail sources. To standardize product metadata across domains, we conducted manual cleaning and enrichment of product features to normalized attribute schemas (e.g. price, material, and style descriptors) using available information from manufacturer and retailer sources. To mimic real-world online retail environments in which human shoppers are able to view multimodal product information, we augment each product entry with images from retail or manufacturer sources. Full details on product inventory construction are in Appendix A . 2.1.2 Persona Construction To simulate diverse and realistic user behaviors, we construct shopper personas by combining real-world grounded profiles with structured preference generation. We initialize personas from the Nemotron-Personas dataset [ 21 ] , which provides large-scale synthetic persona descriptions aligned with real-world demographic and geographic distributions. This ensures coverage of diverse backgrounds and prevents distributional biases. Building on the persona background and age fields of these personas, we synthesize product-specific preferences and dealbreakers that are consistent with the persona to enable controlled evaluation of decision-making behavior. To evaluate robustness under infeasible conditions, we additionally curate a subset of personas whose requirements cannot be satisfied by the available product inventory. Full details on persona construction are in Appendix A.2 . Our persona data statistics are in Appendix A , Table 5 . 2.2 Action Space We model customer-salesperson interaction as a tool-augmented dual-agent system. Shopper Agent Actions: These are terminal actions that end a simulation. • add_to_cart : Accepts a product recommendation. • end_conversation : Exits the interaction without purchase. Salesbot Agent Actions: These tools support grounded recommendations by allowing the sales agent to retrieve products that best fit shopper-specified preferences and dealbreakers. • lookup_buying_guide : Accesses high-level product knowledge, given a natural language query. • lookup_product_items : Retrieves candidate products from the inventory, given a natural language query. We embed product and buying guide and product information with sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 and use the FAISS system [ 11 ] , with top-4 retrieval. Additional details are in Appendix B.1 . 2.3 Evaluation Metrics 2.3.1 Decision Alignment We formalize Decision Alignment as a binary function that evaluates whether a simulated shopper’s final decision is consistent with their latent persona constraints. Let a conversation trajectory be denoted as 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . Let ℛ ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) \mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C}) denote the set of products recommended by the salesbot, a ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ∈ ℛ ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) ∪ { ∅ } a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C})\cup\{\varnothing\} denote the shopper’s final action (i.e., the product added to cart, or ∅ \varnothing if no purchase is made), 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denote the set of acceptable (including ideal) products defined by the shopper’s persona. We then define the decision alignment indicator as: DA ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) = { 1 , if a ( 𝒞 ) ≠ ∅ , and a ( 𝒞 ) ∈ ℛ ( 𝒞 ) , and a ( 𝒞 ) ∈ 𝒜 , 1 , if a ( 𝒞 ) = ∅ , and ℛ ( 𝒞 ) ∩ 𝒜 = ∅ , 0 , otherwise . \mathrm{DA}(\mathcal{C})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if }a(\mathcal{C})\neq\varnothing,\ \text{and }a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C}),\ \text{and }a(\mathcal{C})\in\mathcal{A},\\ 1,&\text{if }a(\mathcal{C})=\varnothing,\ \text{and }\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{C})\cap\mathcal{A}=\emptyset,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (1) The first case captures correct acceptance , where the shopper selects a recommended product that satisfies their constraints. The second case captures correct rejection , where no acceptable options are presented and the shopper abstains from purchasing. All other cases, including accepting unacceptable products or failing to accept acceptable recommendations, are considered misaligned. We report the overall decision alignment rate across all conversations in different product categories as the main metric in our experiments. 2.3.2 Conversational Metrics From real-world customer-salesperson dialogues in Kostric et al. [16] , we observe a number of conversational traits of human shoppers that are significantly different from model generations: (1) Human shoppers tend to only expose general product inquiry with very few requirements at the beginning of the conversation, and gradually expose dealbreakers and preferences throughout the dialogue.
